findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account repairs overspent £2.36m due to increased demand, regulatory requirements, and inflation.
findings.detail: HRA (council housing stock) saw significant £2.36m overspend on responsive repairs alone, attributed to increased demand, regulatory requirements, and inflationary pressures. This suggests either deteriorating stock condition or poor maintenance forecasting, or both.
findings.matters: HRA is a revolving account but unsustainable repair costs indicate asset deterioration or deferred maintenance becoming urgent. For a lender holding HRA debt, this signals underlying asset quality issues.
findings.figures: £2.36m repairs overspend; also £0.367m increase in bad debt provision for rent arrears due to affordability and Universal Credit changes
findings.quote: a significant £2.36m overspend in responsive repairs, reflecting increased demand, regulatory requirements, and inflationary cost pressures, alongside a £0.367m increase in the bad debt provision due to ongoing affordability challenges

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Finance function restructuring underway to address "staffing capacity and capability gaps" but recruitment "historically challenging."
findings.detail: Finance team being restructured below Business Partner level specifically to address staffing capacity and capability gaps. Recruitment is in progress but council notes this "has historically been challenging." This directly relates to the forecasting weakness and suggests resource constraints may be limiting financial control.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity and capability directly impacts budget control, forecasting accuracy, and governance. If recruitment is difficult, the council may be operating with structural finance staff shortages.
findings.figures: No quantification; restructure in progress; vacancies being filled but noted as historically difficult
findings.quote: A restructure of the finance function below the Finance Business Partners level, led by the Director of Finance, is underway to address staffing capacity and capability gaps. Recruitment efforts are in progress to fill vacant posts; however, this has historically been challenging.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Financial forecasting accuracy acknowledged as weak; Q4 overspends not predicted and gap-root-causes identified but not yet resolved.
findings.detail: Council notes "Last year's outturn identified a further overspend emerging in Q4 highlighting weaknesses in the accuracy and timeliness of financial forecasting." Issues stem from gaps in data capture, system reporting, and underlying processes. Work is ongoing but document states "further work is still required." This directly impacts reliability of future projections.
findings.matters: A lender relies on the council's quarterly and forward forecasts. If forecasting is materially inaccurate, the lender cannot rely on the council's projections for medium-term sustainability or budget control.
findings.figures: Forecasting weaknesses across multiple departments; gaps in data capture, system reporting, and processes
findings.quote: Last year's outturn identified a further overspend emerging in Q4 highlighting weaknesses in the accuracy and timeliness of financial forecasting across services. These issues stemmed from gaps in data capture, system reporting, and underlying processes... further work is still required to strengthen forecasting across all areas

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Transformation programme delivered only £8.4m of £10.7m planned savings; reserve investment return below target.
findings.detail: Transformation savings: £8.4m delivered vs £10.7m planned (79%); £0.8m delayed into 2026-27; £1.5m undelivered. Council invested £3.74m reserves for 4:1 target return but forecast return is only £5.6m (below 1.5:1). As programme moves to "more complex, cross‑cutting areas" delivery risk remains.
findings.matters: Medium-term financial plan depends on transformation savings. Under-delivery undermines sustainability forecasts. Below-target ROI on reserve investment means reserves are being consumed, not invested.
findings.figures: £8.4m of £10.7m delivered (79%); £0.8m delayed; £1.5m undelivered; £3.74m reserve invested; £5.6m forecast return vs 4:1 target
findings.quote: At outturn, £8.4m of the £10.7m planned savings from Deficit Recovery Plans and transformation activity have been delivered in 2025/26, with £0.8m delayed into 2026/27 and £1.5m remaining undelivered... Whilst progress has been made and governance arrangements have strengthened, delivery has been mixed across services

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Buckle Close capital project overspent by £3.059m; Denbigh Primary temporary relocation forecast to overspend £1.2m.
findings.detail: Two major capital projects showing delivery issues. Buckle Close represents £3.059m of the £2.964m total Inclusive Growth overspend. Denbigh Primary is forecast to overspend by £1.2m by completion. Both indicate project governance issues.
findings.matters: Individual major project overruns signal poor cost control and risk management. Multiple project overruns suggest systemic issues in scheme governance.
findings.figures: Buckle Close £3.059m overspend; Denbigh Primary £1.2m forecast overspend by completion
findings.quote: This includes forecast overspend relating to Buckle Close of £3.059m and Denbigh Primary temporary relocation £0.809m... Denbigh Primary School which is currently forecast to overspend £1.2m by completion.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Capital governance weak; council lacks assurance over financial implications and sustainability of major schemes.
findings.detail: Council explicitly states "full assurance over the financial implications and long‑term sustainability of these schemes is not yet available" for property acquisition schemes. Final business cases requested but outstanding. This is a direct governance gap the council is flagging.
findings.matters: A lender funds major capital schemes. If the council cannot provide full assurance over affordability, value-for-money, or prudential code compliance at outturn, that is a material governance failure.
findings.figures: Information remains outstanding; full assurance not available
findings.quote: As some information remains outstanding, full assurance over the financial implications and long‑term sustainability of these schemes is not yet available, and strengthened oversight will be critical to mitigating future risks.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Capital programme suffered 70% slippage; £216.1m of £307.2m working budget failed to deliver.
findings.detail: The working budget of £307.2m (after adding £61.8m slippage from prior year) had £216.1m of slippage, leaving only £110m actually spent. Document cites delays in housing, temporary accommodation, regeneration (The Stage) and transport programmes. This scale of slippage indicates systemic delivery issues.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery is a proxy for operational competence. 70% slippage suggests the council cannot manage large projects effectively, which is material to a lender considering major schemes.
findings.figures: £307.2m working budget; £216.1m slippage; £110.0m final outturn
findings.quote: The approved budget as per the Green Book in Feb 2025 of £245.4m was increased by £61.8m of slippage from 2024-25 to give an original working budget of £307.2m. After slippage of £216.1m and the drawing forward of budgets from future years the final budget for the year was £110.0m.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Bad debt provision increased to £1.3m following corporate review; historic debt not being pursued legally.
findings.detail: Council increased bad debt provision significantly after review finding "increased uncertainty of collection, where no legal charges have raised against historic debt." Council has initiated a reactive debt recovery project but this signals collection capability gap and asset quality issue.
findings.matters: Growing bad debt write-offs indicate either weak debtor quality or weak collection practices. A lender needs assurance the council can collect what it is owed, particularly rents and charges.
findings.figures: £1.3m bad debt provision; "no legal charges have raised against historic debt"
findings.quote: At outturn, the bad debt provision was £1.3m. This was increased following a detailed corporate review reflecting increased uncertainty of collection, where no legal charges have raised against historic debt.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspent £2.383m with high-needs and early years blocks both in overspend; deficit funded from brought-forward reserves.
findings.detail: DSG overspent £2.383m in-year: High Needs Block overspent £1.512m and Early Years Block overspent £1.253m. Council absorbed this entirely from brought-forward DSG reserves rather than managing demand. This is a structural grant underfunding issue but the council's response signals inability to control spend.
findings.matters: Schools funding is a pass-through but the council's inability to manage it within grant means it must either cut services or find resources elsewhere. Repeated DSG overspends become a structural budget problem.
findings.figures: £2.383m in-year overspend; £1.512m High Needs Block; £1.253m Early Years Block
findings.quote: the 2025/26 DSG has an in-year overspend of £2.383m, with High Needs Block and Early Years Block overspending by £1.512m and £1.253m respectively

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Children's services overspend structural and unresolved at £5.842m despite deficit recovery plan.
findings.detail: Children's services overspent by £5.842m (8.4% of budget), primarily from high-cost placements. The overspend increased by £0.364m since Q3, showing the trend worsening, not improving. This is a demand-led service the council must provide and cannot avoid.
findings.matters: Structural overspends in essential services represent unfunded liabilities. A lender must know if the council can fund its core statutory duties or if this becomes an ongoing call on borrowing.
findings.figures: £5.842m overspend (8.4%); £5.580m from high-cost placements; trend worsening (£0.364m deterioration since Q3)
findings.quote: Children's Services – Outturn overspend £5.842m (8.4%) against budget £69.282m, an increase of £0.364m since Q3. The main contributors for the overspend are £5.580m in children social care placements driven primarily by high-cost placements

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A- 2025-26 Provisional Revenue and Capital Outturn Report
findings.headline: Council achieved balanced position only by releasing contingency and drawing reserves, masking underlying stress.
findings.detail: Q3 showed a £6.7m projected overspend. The final balanced position required releasing all £6.6m contingency plus an additional £1.2m drawdown from general fund reserves. This means the underlying operational position remains stressed and only appears balanced through one-time reserve usage.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if the council is genuinely managing finances or using reserves to paper over structural problems. Reserve-funded balance is unsustainable and signals future difficulty.
findings.figures: £6.7m Q3 overspend projected; £6.6m contingency released; £1.2m reserve drawdown
findings.quote: Note the release of £6.6m contingency to address pressures in demand-led services and one-off exceptional items during 2025/26. Note the £1.2m additional drawdown from earmarked General Fund reserves

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Overall control environment is only 'adequate', not 'substantial'—meaning weaknesses put objectives at risk—with only 69% of audits resulting in acceptable assurance
findings.detail: The Audit Manager's overall opinion is that 'an adequate level of assurance can be provided in connection with the council's overall control environment.' The audit opinion scale defines adequate as 'there are weaknesses that put a minority of the system objectives at risk.' Of 43 audits completed, 69% resulted in acceptable assurance (adequate or above), meaning 31% identified significant control concerns. The report states 'the audit reviews that have presented significant concern relate to specific parts of the Council, and it is important that the recommendations made to improve control are implemented in order for a continued acceptable assurance opinion to be given.'
findings.matters: The council is not scoring strongly on its own audit opinion. An 'adequate' rather than 'substantial' opinion means the auditors have identified meaningful control weaknesses. A lender would interpret this as elevated risk.
findings.figures: 69% acceptable assurance (adequate or above); 31% of audits showing concern
findings.quote: Based on the areas of assessment detailed in Section 3 above, whilst there are concerns on some areas, I am satisfied that an 'adequate' level of assurance can be provided in connection with the council's overall control environment.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Pre-payment card system for direct payments to families cannot distinguish which child within a family received which funds, creating audit and accountability risk
findings.detail: The pre-payment card audit found that 'the system does not clearly distinguish payments made to the same family for different children where only one prepayment card was issued.' Management have now identified that a review is needed of all pre-payment cards issued prior to June 2024 where only one card served multiple children, to establish whether funds can be traced to the intended child. Since June 2024, new cards are being issued individually.
findings.matters: A lender funding children's services needs to know that for at least two years, the council could not verify that direct payments to families were spent on the intended child. This is both a controls issue and a safeguarding concern.
findings.figures: Affecting all pre-payment cards issued prior to June 2024 where one card served multiple children
findings.quote: We noted the system does not clearly distinguish payments made to the same family for different children where only one prepayment card was issued. This limits assurance that funds are allocated and used appropriately for each child in accordance with their individual care plan.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Mobile phone expenditure significantly exceeded budget in both 2024/25 and 2025/26, indicating ongoing budget control failure
findings.detail: The Mobile Phones audit (May 2026) noted that 'mobile telephony expenditure had significantly exceeded budget in both 2024/25 and 2025/26.' Additional control issues included 6 out of 10 sampled staff leavers still showing as active device holders on the asset register, and incomplete financial coding creating suspense account entries requiring manual work to clear.
findings.matters: A lender assesses budget discipline. Two consecutive years of uncontrolled mobile phone overspends suggest the council is not tracking or managing departmental spend effectively, a broader indicator of financial control weakness.
findings.figures: Overbudget both 2024/25 and 2025/26; 6 of 10 leavers still active on register
findings.quote: In addition, we noted mobile telephony expenditure had significantly exceeded budget in both 2024/25 and 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: VAT partial exemption calculation has not been undertaken for seven years; if the 5% (£7,500) threshold is breached, the council must repay ALL VAT on exempt activities, not just the excess
findings.detail: The VAT audit found that HMRC's annual partial exemption calculation—which determines whether Luton can claim input VAT—had not been completed for seven years at the time of the audit. The audit noted: 'If the threshold is breached the council is required to repay all VAT relating to exempt activities (not just the excess above 5%).' An external VAT advisor has now been engaged to complete the calculation for 2024/25 and submit to HMRC, but the seven-year gap creates material exposure to potential HMRC enforcement.
findings.matters: A seven-year compliance failure on a statutory calculation creates exposure to potential HMRC penalties and forced repayment of VAT claims. A lender needs to know about latent tax liabilities.
findings.figures: 7 years without completion; 5% (or £7,500) threshold
findings.quote: HMRC requires local authorities to complete partial exemption calculations annually to confirm how much of their input tax has been claimed on exempt supplies. Local authorities will benefit from input VAT related activities that is below the threshold of 5% (or £7,500). If the threshold is breached the council is required to repay all VAT relating to exempt activities (not just the excess above 5%). At the time of the audit, this annual calculation had not been undertaken for seven years.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Icknield Primary School receives 'No Assurance' rating—the worst audit opinion available—meaning control is poor and the system is open to significant error or abuse
findings.detail: Of 43 audit reviews conducted, only one received the worst audit opinion category. Icknield Primary School's audit identified 'a significant number of internal control weaknesses particularly in relation to governance, financial planning, monitoring and control, purchasing, income, payroll and personnel, asset management and data security.' The auditors found 'control is poor, leaving the system open to significant error or abuse' and raised 9 high-priority, 35 medium-priority, and 8 low-priority recommendations.
findings.matters: A lender funding the council needs to know that money flowing to at least one council school has virtually no financial controls in place. The 'No Assurance' rating is the audit opinion reserved for systems that could fail materially.
findings.figures: 1 out of 43 audits received No Assurance; 9 high priority, 35 medium priority, 8 low priority recommendations at Icknield
findings.quote: We found control was poor, leaving the system open to significant error or abuse and/or significant non-compliance with basic controls. Based on the areas reviewed we issued a 'No' assurance opinion.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Accounts Receivable system failure has forced emergency admin access across the whole team, creating fraud and data integrity risk
findings.detail: In February 2026, a system upgrade broke the Accounts Receivable application, creating 'a substantial increase in the need for manual intervention'. From mid-March 2026, Luton granted admin access to the entire Accounts Receivable team as a temporary workaround. This emergency measure persists and 'increases the risk of unauthorised access, fraud and irregularity, and unintended changes' to the system.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that a core financial system used to track council income is operating under emergency controls with elevated fraud risk and data integrity concerns.
findings.figures: From mid-March 2026; admin access granted to whole Accounts Receivable team
findings.quote: The upgrade issues associated with the application led to a substantial increase in the need for manual intervention and, as a temporary workaround from mid-March 2026, admin access was granted to the whole Accounts Receivable team. Extending elevated access to a wider group of users increases the risk of unauthorised access, fraud and irregularity, and unintended changes within the Accounts Receivable module, which could affect data integrity and lead to financial misstatement.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix B - Corporate Risk Register Update
findings.headline: Disproportionate Home Office asylum placements are creating unplanned demand pressures on social care, housing and education services
findings.detail: Council reports it is receiving a disproportionate share of asylum seeker placements from the Home Office, creating risks to safeguarding and placing pressures on high-cost services. Council established new Asylum Board in February 2026 specifically to manage cost and prevention risks. Pressures are ongoing and explicitly described as threats to core services.
findings.matters: Adds uncontracted demand to high-cost services (social care, housing) during period of budget deficit; cost control depends on Home Office management of placements outside council's direct control.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: Disproportionate asylum seeker numbers accommodated within LA. Risks around 1. safeguarding and service support for those placed in Luton by the Home Office and 2. risks to increased service delivery pressures on core services such as social care, education, health and housing

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix B - Corporate Risk Register Update
findings.headline: Luton Rising airport company faces financial sustainability risk from traffic decline, which could increase council's debt exposure as shareholder
findings.detail: Council-owned airport company faces potential revenue reduction from operational incidents, force majeure events or passenger decline. Airport expansion programme is also at risk of delay. Any revenue shortfall reduces returns to council and increases exposure to company debt.
findings.matters: Council has financial exposure as shareholder; airport generates expected revenues and returns that may not materialise; expansion delays affect council's growth strategy.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: There is a risk that Luton Rising's financial sustainability is adversely impacted by a decrease in airport income associated with (for example), a major operational incident, special force majeure event or decline in air passengers. The airport's expansion could also be affected by delay or suspension of the airport expansion programme and the airport's future commercial model. This could reduce expected revenues and returns to the Council and increase financial exposure from Luton Rising's debt

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix B - Corporate Risk Register Update
findings.headline: Council's operational estate is deteriorating due to revenue and capital budget constraints, creating building compliance and energy cost risks
findings.detail: Progressive dilapidation of operational buildings from budget cuts creates risks of non-compliance with building regulations and rising energy costs. Council has an Estate Rationalisation Plan and is updating Asset Management Plan, with planned major investment in Town Hall, but the register indicates cuts have already caused deterioration.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance typically signals financial stress and future unfunded liabilities; energy cost increases could add to revenue pressures.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: Progressive dilapidation and deterioration of our operational estate due to both revenue and capital budget cuts, leading to the risk of building non-compliance and increased energy costs impacting on service delivery

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix B - Corporate Risk Register Update
findings.headline: Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) service demand is growing faster than the council can manage, driving higher costs
findings.detail: Increasing requests for statutory assessment are causing delays and cost increases. The council was managing this as a specific budget pressure in 2025/26 that required additional growth allocation in 2026/27 to achieve a sustainable budget. Council is investing in preventative services to reduce specialist placement demand.
findings.matters: SEND is a high-cost, demand-led statutory service; unmanaged growth directly contributed to 2025/26 deficit and continues to create budget pressure.
findings.figures: None disclosed; identified as significant budget pressure in 2025/26 requiring additional growth in 2026/27
findings.quote: Inability to manage demand for Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) services due to increasing requests for statutory assessment, resulting in delays to decision making, increased costs, and adverse impacts on children and young people's education and outcomes... The 2026/27 budget includes additional growth to address the budget pressure declared in children services in 2025/26 to achieve a more robust and sustainable budget

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix B - Corporate Risk Register Update
findings.headline: Foxhall Homes (council-owned housing company) is unable to service debt and faces potential loss of council equity investment due to construction cost overruns and delivery delays
findings.detail: Rising construction costs, delivery delays and contractor administrations have threatened the company's financial viability. The company could face inability to repay council loans, loss of the council's equity position, and failure to deliver planned housing schemes. Council has established oversight through Shareholders Group and escalation via Gateway Framework.
findings.matters: Council has direct financial exposure as equity investor and creditor; any default would crystallise losses and reduce housing delivery against council strategy.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: Foxhall Homes' financial sustainability has been challenged by external pressures, including rising construction costs, delivery delays and contractor administrations. This could lead to an inability to service debt and repay Council loans, loss of the Council's equity investment, and non-delivery of planned housing schemes, potentially resulting in additional financial exposure for the Council as shareholder

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix B - Corporate Risk Register Update
findings.headline: Council implemented a two-year deficit recovery plan after a significant budget deficit in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council experienced material budget deficits in 2025/26 driven by demand pressures in social care, homelessness, SEND and supported living. While the 2026/27 budget is balanced, the council is implementing a multi-year recovery plan. Recent government finance settlement provided additional funding for core statutory services, improving the position.
findings.matters: Indicates structural demand-driven pressures that extend beyond 2026/27; council financial sustainability depends on ongoing government funding and delivery of savings plans.
findings.figures: 2025/26 deficit amount not specified; 2026/27 budget balanced
findings.quote: increase in demand in areas such as social care, homelessness, SEND, and supported living has resulted in a significant budget deficit for 2025/26 and is subject to specific challenges and risks... the council is updating its mitigation plans and will regularly monitor and report corrective measures to address and assist the council to deliver a balanced budget this year including a deficit recovery plan that will extend over two years

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 2 - 2025-26 Volatile Budget Monitoring Q4 for Outturn
findings.headline: Adult social care demand sustained across learning disability, physical disability and home care services
findings.detail: Learning disability placements increased 36 clients with average weekly cost rising £32. Physical disability placements increased 9 with costs rising £91 per week. Home care packages continue to grow driven by hospital discharges (Better Care Fund funded initially) plus demographics and acuity of health needs. Direct payments increasing with average weekly cost up £42 per client.
findings.matters: Sustained growth across multiple adult social care lines indicates demographic and acuity-driven cost pressures that will persist regardless of operational efficiency.
findings.figures: Learning disability +9 clients, weekly cost +£32; Physical disability +9 clients, weekly cost +£91; Home care numbers increasing; Direct payments +20 clients, weekly cost +£42
findings.quote: Increasing demographics and acuity of health needs have contributed to increased costs.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 2 - 2025-26 Volatile Budget Monitoring Q4 for Outturn
findings.headline: HRA responsive repairs overspend of £2.72m accompanied by rise in disrepair claims
findings.detail: Responsive repairs are showing circa £2.72m overspend against HRA budget. BTS (the council's repairs contractor) reports a rise in disrepair claims. The commentary notes this "needs to be managed to ensure that residents are complying with tenancy agreements, and that the repairs reflect the condition of the stock."
findings.matters: Rising disrepair claims indicate potential deterioration of the housing stock and represent landlord liability exposure that is not adequately reflected in budgets.
findings.figures: £2.72m overspend against HRA budget; rising disrepair claims trend
findings.quote: BTS reports that there has been a rise in disrepair claims. An overspend in the cost of repairs of circa £2.72m against the HRA budget. This increase needs to be managed to ensure that residents are complying with tenancy agreements, and that the repairs reflect the condition of the stock.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 2 - 2025-26 Volatile Budget Monitoring Q4 for Outturn
findings.headline: Children's residential and semi-independent placements accelerating with both rising numbers and unit costs
findings.detail: Residential LAC marked RED status with continued increases in both demand and weekly costs from providers. The 16+ semi-independent cohort has expanded by 10 FTE since March 2025 and a further 3 FTE since Q2. Non-LAC leaving care is overspending by 20% against budget.
findings.matters: Accelerating placement numbers and costs in children's services indicate sustained demographic/social need pressure that will compound if not addressed, with no visibility of when demand will plateau.
findings.figures: 16+ semi-independent +10 FTE since March 2025; Non-LAC leaving care 20% overspend
findings.quote: Residential placements have seen a continued increase in both demand and weekly costs from providers, high cost reviews are ongoing to check suitability of placements with a view to stepping down where appropriate

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 2 - 2025-26 Volatile Budget Monitoring Q4 for Outturn
findings.headline: BTS Trading Services forecasting £2.7m deficit in 2025-26 due to Buckle Close construction defects
findings.detail: The council's BTS trading company has encountered construction defects on the Buckle Close HRA development. Q4 outturn shows a further £1.223m overspend, driven by £0.332m of additional costs on Buckle Close (portable offices and roofing works) plus £0.726m from supplies/services overruns and income shortfalls.
findings.matters: A £2.7m deficit on the council's own trading operation represents a direct drain on council resources and indicates operational control issues with a capital project.
findings.figures: £2.7m deficit forecast for 2025/26; Q4 additional overspend £1.223m (£0.332m Buckle Close, £0.726m other)
findings.quote: BTS has worked on the Buckle Close development for HRA and the forecast £2.7m deficit in 2025/26 recognises the construction defects that occurred.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Investment income of £44.9m (29% of council borrowing costs) dependent on LLAL debenture interest and interest rates, creating treasury vulnerability
findings.detail: The council generated £44.9m interest income in 2025/26, including £41.7m from Luton Living Accommodation Limited (LLAL) debenture. This income is critical to offsetting borrowing costs of £16.7m. The report notes this reflects 'higher interest rate environment' and that income remains 'sensitive to both cashflow levels and underlying market activity.' This creates significant exposure to interest rate falls.
findings.matters: Interest income is volatile and cannot be relied upon if rates fall. If investment income reduces, the council's borrowing costs become exposed and the budget will not balance.
findings.figures: Total interest income £44.9m (£1.1m above budget); LLAL debenture interest £41.7m (£0.565m above budget); borrowing costs £16.7m. Income outperformed budget due to SONIA-based rates post-LIBOR abolition.
findings.quote: The most significant contributor to investment income remains LLAL debenture interest of £41.7m at outturn (£0.565m increase against budget), which has outperformed budget due to application of SONIA -based rates since the abolition of LIBOR.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £216.1m (70% of original budget) with major delays on housing, The Stage, and highways
findings.detail: Of the £307.2m original working capital budget, £216.1m slipped into future years (70% slippage rate). Key slippage: housing £55.4m, The Stage £40.7m, highways £17.5m, transport £9.2m. This level of slippage indicates project delivery capability issues and will compress future years' capital programmes.
findings.matters: Large slippage defers expenditure but also suggests delays in delivering promised outcomes (new housing, regeneration schemes, highways) and creates cashflow and financing uncertainty.
findings.figures: £216.1m capital slippage out of £307.2m working budget (70%). Slippage items: housing £55.4m, The Stage £40.7m, highways £17.5m, transport £9.2m, four other Inclusive Growth projects £12m.
findings.quote: The key slippage items relate primarily to Housing projects (£55.4m), The Stage (£40.7m), Highways (£17.5m), Transport Programme (£9.2m), and £12m relating to four other Inclusive Growth projects.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account responsive repairs overspent £2.36m (28% of budget) due to Awaab's Law compliance and disrepair liability
findings.detail: HRA reactive repairs overspent by £2.36m (actual £10.696m vs budget £8.336m, a 28% overspend). The council attributes this to 'shift towards more comprehensive and durable repairs rather than short-term fixes, increased disrepair activity leading to higher legal and accelerated repair costs, regulatory requirements such as Awaab's Law requiring faster response times and increased contractor usage.' This is expected to continue.
findings.matters: Awaab's Law compliance is now mandatory. If current budgets cannot accommodate required response times and repair standards, the council faces either continuing overspends or regulatory breach.
findings.figures: £2.36m reactive repairs overspend: actual £10.696m vs budget £8.336m (28% over). Spend to 31 March 2026 includes higher contractor usage and legal costs from disrepair claims.
findings.quote: The overall position reflects a £2.36m overspend on HRA Reactive Repairs (Actual £10.696m vs Budget £8.336m), driven by, a shift towards mo re comprehensive and durable repairs rather than short -term fixes, increased disrepair activity leading to higher legal and accelerated repair costs, regulatory requirements such as Awaab's Law requiring faster response times and increased contractor usage

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspend of £2.383m driven by £1.512m High Needs Block pressure, with no solution identified
findings.detail: DSG overspent by £2.383m in 2025/26. The High Needs Block alone overspent by £1.512m despite a 0.3% transfer from Schools Block (£0.724m). The Early Years Block overspent by £1.253m partly due to timing differences in DfE adjustments. The council notes increased take-up of 2-year-old and under-2 entitlements but funding adjustments have not yet been received.
findings.matters: DSG is ring-fenced but deficits carry forward. A £1.512m High Needs overspend that persists despite shifting funding from Schools Block suggests either demand forecasting failure or insufficient funding from DfE.
findings.figures: DSG outturn overspend £2.383m: High Needs Block £1.512m, Early Years Block £1.253m. 0.3% transfer from Schools Block to HNB = £0.724m. 2-year-old take-up increased 19.86% and under-2s by 4.77%.
findings.quote: At th e end of financial year 2025/26  DSG has an in- year overspend of £2.383m  against budget , with High Needs Block and Early Years Block overspending by £1.512m and £1.253m respectively

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Finance team workforce instability: £0.963m agency overspend due to high turnover and unfilled permanent posts
findings.detail: The council's Accountancy team is experiencing staffing crisis with £0.963m net employee overspend driven by agency cover for vacant posts during recruitment and £0.417m of agency support on statutory tasks. The report notes 'key staff departures within the Accountancy team, driven by retirement and career progression' and 'recruitment remains challenging in a highly competitive market.' Management plans to recruit permanent staff and review middle management structure in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A finance team unable to fill permanent posts is a governance weakness and creates statutory risk. Reliance on agencies for statutory financial tasks (audit, accounts, benefits) is unsustainable and expensive.
findings.figures: £0.963m net employee overspend in Accountancy; £0.602m for agency cover of vacant posts; £0.417m for agency support on statutory tasks (partly offset by £0.215m MHCLG funding). Additional growth of £0.54m agreed for 2026/27 finance resources.
findings.quote: Accountancy employee net  overspend of £0.963 m comprising of £ 0.602m for agency cover of vacant posts during recruitment (including estimated recruitment costs), £0.417m for agency support on statutory tasks (partly offset by £ 0.215m MHCLG funding)

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Transformation programme delivering at ROI of 1.3 against target of 4:1, with £1.5m of planned 2025/26 savings undelivered
findings.detail: The council set a 4:1 return on investment target for the transformation programme. As of March 2026, actual ROI is 1.3. Of £10.7m planned savings for 2025/26, only £8.4m was delivered, with £1.5m undelivered. The report flags concerns: 'there remain concerns regarding the robustness and maturity of some business cases developed as part of the 2026/27 budget setting process.'
findings.matters: Savings targets are critical to the council's MTFP. Delivering at one-third of expected ROI and missing £1.5m of planned savings in a single year suggests either poor planning or delivery challenges that will extend into 2026/27 onwards.
findings.figures: £10.675m savings budgeted for 2025/26; £8.416m delivered; £0.790m delayed to 2026/27; £1.468m undelivered. ROI 1.3 vs target 4:1. Expenditure on transformation projects £2.585m with £3.352m savings forecast across 24/25–26/27.
findings.quote: Whilst early delivery has achieved tangible savings of £1. 0m and there are clear improvements in programme governance, benefits tracking, and accountability, the early delivered return on investment of 1.3  is materially reduced from initial expectations of 4

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Denbigh Primary emergency school relocation project now forecast £2.477m over approved budget with no funding solution identified
findings.detail: Executive approved £9.871m in January 2026 for emergency Denbigh Primary works and temporary site relocation. Forecast cost to completion has risen to £12.348m (£2.477m overspend). The report states 'additional savings or underspends will need to be identified to avoid the need for additional borrowing' and that 'a further report will be presented to Executive to address the increased costs and proposed funding arrangements.' No funding solution is yet confirmed.
findings.matters: An emergency capital project with unresolved funding is a red flag. The council is still seeking funding solutions and cannot yet confirm how the overspend will be financed.
findings.figures: Original approval £9.871m, forecast completion £12.348m, overspend £2.477m (Bishopscote Road temporary site £1.206m, Denbigh Primary capital works £1.271m). Spend to 31 March 2026 was £7.571m.
findings.quote: The total forecast cost to completion is now £12.348m, representing an overall increase of  £2.477m compared to the original approval. This variance includes  £1.206m attributable to the Bishopscote Road site and £1.271m relating to Denbigh Primary School.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs remain volatile and structurally unaffordable despite £6m budget growth for 2026/27
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £5.842m (8.4% of £69.282m budget). Placement costs overspent by £5.580m despite only 320 children in care (down from 420 two years ago), driven by semi-independent accommodation and residential care. The council is receiving £6m growth in base budget for 2026/27 'to ensure no pressure from 2025/26 is carried forward,' indicating current budget is insufficient.
findings.matters: A statutory service cannot sustainably operate with placement costs rising despite fewer children in care. Growth in base budget to cover 2025/26 pressures is a structural admission the budget was not set correctly.
findings.figures: £5.842m overspend (8.4%); placement costs £5.580m over budget; only 320 children in care vs 420 two years ago; £6.000m growth funding approved for 2026/27
findings.quote: Children's social care placements are overspent by £5.580m. This includes home care packages and care leavers accommodation, both of which continue to rise. Despite the number of children in care being low (320 currently, down from 420 two years ago), the cost of care continues to increase.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 - Detailed 2025-26 Provisional Outturn Report_10.06.2026_ FOR EXEC FINAL
findings.headline: Balanced position achieved only through contingency drawdown and reserves, masking underlying service pressures
findings.detail: The council reported a £6.7m projected overspend at Q3 but reached a balanced position by applying £6.6m of contingency and £0.154m of reserves to address pressures in demand-led services. The report explicitly states these were used 'to address pressures in demand-led services and one-off exceptional items,' indicating the structural budget did not balance.
findings.matters: Lenders need to see a sustainable underlying budget position, not balances achieved through one-off contingencies. Repeated reliance on reserves signals structural unaffordability in service provision.
findings.figures: £6.6m contingency released, £0.154m reserves used, from £17.6.1m revenue budget; net improvement of £6.7m from Q3 position
findings.quote: The final provisional outturn for the 2025/26 General Fund indicates a balanced position against the approved £17 6.1m revenue budget. This is a net improvement of £ 6.7m compared to the projected overspend of  £6.7m reported at Q3. This reflects the application of £6.6m of contingency and £0.154m of reserves to address pressures in demand-led services and one-off exceptional items.

findings.paper_title: 7 - Appendix A - Corporate Performance Report Annual 2025-26 - OSB 15 06 26
findings.headline: Local procurement spend is 47.2% against a 60% target — a 13-point miss indicating either market-level constraint or contracting effectiveness issues.
findings.detail: Luton's 'Grow Local' procurement target requires 60% of influenceable spend to go to local suppliers within 20 miles of Town Hall. The council ended at 47.2%, a significant gap. While the top three suppliers increased spend by 27%, this was insufficient to reach target. The council attributes the miss to 'market instability' and plans to engage with local markets earlier.
findings.matters: A consistent miss on procurement targets can indicate either that the council has weak leverage with its supplier base or that local market capacity is constrained. Either reveals something about local economic conditions, the council's purchasing power, or its ability to shape the market.
findings.quote: However, the Grow Local spend is still below the Luton Borough Council target of 60%.

findings.paper_title: 7 - Appendix A - Corporate Performance Report Annual 2025-26 - OSB 15 06 26
findings.headline: Care leavers in suitable accommodation are 5 percentage points below target (84.8% vs 90%), with explicit challenges for those with complex needs or custody discharge.
findings.detail: The council missed its care leavers accommodation target and explicitly identifies gaps for young people with complex needs and those leaving custody. The service notes ongoing challenges in accessing housing options and coordinating multiagency support, suggesting coordination or commissioning issues.
findings.matters: This is a safeguarding duty. Young people in unsuitable housing create liability risk and can lead to costly crisis interventions. The gap suggests either housing market constraints or problems coordinating with partners — both material to financial planning.
findings.figures: 84.8% actual vs 90% target
findings.quote: The current gap to target suggests ongoing challenges in accessing suitable accommodation, particularly for care leavers with complex needs or those who may be discharged from custody where housing options can be more limited and require enhanced support and multiagency coordination.

findings.paper_title: 7 - Appendix A - Corporate Performance Report Annual 2025-26 - OSB 15 06 26
findings.headline: HR check-in compliance is only 53% against target of 80%, indicating weak people management and governance control.
findings.detail: Check-in compliance — tracking regular performance conversations between managers and staff — is significantly below target at 52.81%. The council acknowledges incomplete recording but this remains a governance weakness. Weak people management is often a leading indicator of broader organizational control issues.
findings.matters: Check-ins are a foundational HR control for managing performance, identifying problems early, and maintaining accountability. Only 53% compliance suggests management may not have visibility into staff performance, workload, or morale — red flags for an organization managing a major budget.
findings.figures: 52.81% actual vs 80% target
findings.quote: While not all check-ins are being recorded on iTrent, this figure represents a continued improvement.

findings.paper_title: 7 - Appendix A - Corporate Performance Report Annual 2025-26 - OSB 15 06 26
findings.headline: Carers receiving statutory reviews are only 40.3% of caseload against a 55% target, signalling persistent social care capacity problems.
findings.detail: The proportion of carers receiving reviews has not improved to target despite actions. The council acknowledges being approximately 15% below target at year end. This parallels the adult review backlog and indicates systemic understaffing or management issues in social care commissioning.
findings.matters: Carers are co-deliverers of care and must be reviewed to assess their own wellbeing and support needs. A 15-point miss on this metric suggests the council is not managing its social care partnerships effectively, which could indicate broader commissioning and financial planning weakness.
findings.figures: 40.3% actual vs 55% target; approximately 15 percentage points below expected target
findings.quote: We have ended quarter 4 approx. 15% below our expected target.

findings.paper_title: 7 - Appendix A - Corporate Performance Report Annual 2025-26 - OSB 15 06 26
findings.headline: Adult social care annual reviews are 11 percentage points below target at year end, indicating capacity or management issues in a major spending area.
findings.detail: Luton ended 2025-26 with 79.1% of adult social care recipients receiving an annual review against a target of 90%. Performance declined in Q4 and the council acknowledges a backlog. This is a statutory duty — failing to deliver reviews at the required rate could hide unmet needs, additional costs, or indicate broader capacity problems affecting other council functions.
findings.matters: Annual reviews in adult social care are a statutory requirement. Systematic backlogs suggest either understaffing or management control issues, both of which could affect the council's ability to manage its financial position and plan spending accurately.
findings.figures: 79.1% actual vs 90% target; 11% under target in Q4
findings.quote: The proportion of annual reviews has completed at an average of 11% under target in quarter 4.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Annual (Outturn) Report
findings.headline: Investment portfolio shrunk 43% following strategic shift away from external borrowing
findings.detail: Liquid investments held by the council fell from £33.119m at 31 March 2025 to £18.766m at 31 March 2026, a reduction of £14.353m. This reflects the council's decision to use internal cash balances in place of external borrowing, reducing both investment holdings and investment income generation.
findings.matters: A shrinking investment portfolio reduces the council's liquidity buffer and cash-flow flexibility. In a refinancing shock—such as unexpected debt maturity—the council has £14m less accessible funds than the prior year.
findings.figures: Investments fell from £33.119m to £18.766m; achieved average return of 4.926% on internally managed funds
findings.quote: The use of internal borrowing has reduced the level of investments held during the year and therefore the level of investment income generated.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Annual (Outturn) Report
findings.headline: Rising borrowing costs explicitly flagged as risk to viability of uncommenced capital schemes
findings.detail: The council states: 'There remains a risk that rising borrowing costs could impact the affordability of elements of the capital programme, particularly for schemes not yet commenced.' This is not prospective hedging language—it names a specific threat to capital delivery. The council expects to conduct 'ongoing review and appraisal' of which schemes remain affordable.
findings.matters: This is the council's own statement that it may not be able to afford its planned capital investment if borrowing costs remain elevated. For a lender, this means either projects will be shelved (affecting local economy and asset base) or the council will seek alternative funding or deferral.
findings.figures: Non-HRA financing cost ratio rose to 13.43% (2025/26 actual vs 11.82% in 2024/25); Arlingclose forecasts Bank Rate held at 3.75% near term with upside risks
findings.quote: There remains a risk that rising borrowing costs could impact the affordability of elements of the capital programme, particularly for schemes not yet commenced, and these will continue to be subject to ongoing review and appraisal.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Annual (Outturn) Report
findings.headline: Council holds under-borrowed position of £177m while suddenly shifting £64m HRA debt to longer-term fixed funding
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, Luton's borrowing (£844.984m) fell £177.221m short of its Capital Financing Requirement (£1,022.205m). The shortfall is funded by internal cash balances. However, in February 2026, £64m of maturing HRA debt was urgently refinanced through PWLB instead of being rolled in the short-term money markets, following geopolitical escalation and increased market volatility.
findings.matters: An under-borrowed strategy depends on available cash and stable short-term rates. The shift to fixed-rate PWLB funding for HRA debt—described as necessary for 'stability'—signals the council views short-term rates as unattractive and is concerned about further volatility. Future borrowing to fund the remaining £177m under-borrowed position will face higher rates.
findings.figures: Under-borrowed position £177.221m; £64m HRA refinanced to PWLB; short-term borrowing fell from £58.0m to £46.9m
findings.quote: market conditions became more volatile during the year, initially following the introduction of US trade tariffs in April 2025 and subsequently due to the escalation of conflict in the Middle East in February 2026. These events materially increased uncertainty around inflation and the future path of interest rates. In response, £64m of maturing HRA debt was refinanced through the PWLB to provide greater stability

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Annual (Outturn) Report
findings.headline: Planned capital programme delivered at only 43% of budget, with major schemes delayed into 2026/27
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure was budgeted at £204.070m but only £86.874m was actually spent in 2025/26. The council specifically names housing projects, The Stage, highways and the transport programme as schemes that experienced delays and were reprofiled to future years. This signals sustained delivery risk on the council's capital investment plan.
findings.matters: Persistent underspend against capital budgets raises questions about project management, planning permissions, or financial capacity to execute the capital strategy. For a lender, this affects both the timing of borrowing need and whether planned assets will materialise.
findings.figures: General Fund budgeted £204.070m, actual £86.874m (43% delivery); HRA budgeted £39.622m, actual £23.122m (58% delivery)
findings.quote: A significant proportion of the planned capital programme was reprofiled during 2025/26 due to delays in several major schemes, including housing projects, The Stage, highways and the transport programme.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Significant funding uncertainty beyond 2028/29 settlement with potential funding cliff edge
findings.detail: The MTFP faces significant uncertainty beyond the 2026/27-2028/29 multi-year settlement period. Post-2028/29 funding assumptions remain subject to uncertainty and include exposure to Fair Funding Review 2.0, business rates retention changes, and a potential 'funding cliff edge'. The council has retained pre-2028/29 funding assumptions in the refresh as a placeholder pending Government announcements.
findings.matters: For a lender, funding reform risk after 2028/29 creates contingent liability for the council; the budget gaps could worsen significantly if the funding settlement is less favourable than assumed.
findings.figures: Multi-year settlement covers 2026/27-2028/29 only; post-2028/29 assumptions retained pending Government announcements
findings.quote: Reliance on current funding mechanisms and transitional protections; exposure to post-2028/29 funding uncertainty and wider Government funding reform

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Core financial assumptions flagged as increasingly exposed to risk and requiring strengthening
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states that 'several of the core assumptions underpinning the approved MTFP are increasingly exposed to risk and require further strengthening through service-led validation and mitigation plans.' These include demand stabilisation, pay/workforce costs exceeding 3%, inflation above assumptions, funding uncertainty, national policy reforms, and savings delivery risk.
findings.matters: Multiple core planning assumptions are acknowledged as at risk; this signals the MTFP is built on shakier foundations than originally approved and will likely require substantial revision.
findings.figures: Pay assumption revised from 3.0% to 3.3% for 2026/27; inflation assumptions increased to 3.5-4.3% effective rate
findings.quote: These factors indicate that several of the core assumptions underpinning the approved MTFP are increasingly exposed to risk and require further strengthening through service-led validation and mitigation plans.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Savings delivery becoming more challenging as programmes grow more complex
findings.detail: While the council delivered £8.4m of £10.7m savings in 2025/26 (78%), the paper notes that delivery of £10.95m savings in 2026/27 'remains challenging as programmes become more complex and cross-cutting in nature'. No savings are identified in the MTFP from 2028/29 onwards, with the implication that the council may not have further transformation capacity.
findings.matters: Declining savings delivery rate and lack of identified savings from 2028/29 onwards means the council is relying on growth assumptions and demand modelling to close gaps, rather than controllable cost reductions.
findings.figures: £8.4m of £10.7m delivered in 2025/26 (78%); £10.95m required in 2026/27; no identified savings from 2028/29 to 2031/32
findings.quote: Whilst the Council delivered £8.4m of the £10.7m savings programme in 2025/26 through DRPs and transformation activity, delivery of savings in 2026/27 remains challenging as programmes become more complex and cross-cutting in nature

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant moving into deficit in 2027/28 with potential transfer to General Fund
findings.detail: Current expenditure trends indicate DSG will move into deficit in 2027/28. The MTFP assumes the statutory override continues until 2027/28 with no General Fund impact, but if the override ends or national arrangements change, DSG deficits could transfer to the General Fund, creating a significant additional financial pressure.
findings.matters: DSG deficits present a contingent liability; if the statutory override is removed, this could add several million pounds of unplanned pressure to the General Fund.
findings.figures: DSG expected to move into deficit in 2027/28
findings.quote: Current expenditure trends indicate that the Dedicated Schools Grant is expected to move into deficit in 2027/28. The MTFP assumes that the statutory override continues until 2027/28, with no General Fund impact. However, if the override ends or national arrangements change without a sustainable funding solution, DSG deficits could transfer to the General Fund, creating a significant additional financial pressure for the Council.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Multiple service-level emerging risks remain unquantified and require further assessment
findings.detail: The paper identifies multiple emerging service-specific issues that have not yet been quantified: ASC market sustainability pressures, Employment Rights Act Fair Pay Agreements implications, Public Health ringfencing constraints, Homelessness Prevention Grant funding reductions, Awaabs Law extension costs, and SEND assessment pressures. These are flagged as requiring 'further assessment and validation' during budget development.
findings.matters: Unquantified risks in multiple service areas create uncertainty about the true scale of budget pressures; these could materially worsen the identified gaps when quantified.
findings.figures: £0.5m Public Health contribution to wider services under review; 53 papers unreadable; multiple pressures identified but not quantified
findings.quote: In addition to the risks set out above, several emerging service-specific issues have been identified through the MTFP refresh process which require further assessment and validation as part of the 2027/28 Budget and 2027–32 MTFP development process. It is important to note that these risks have not been quantified yet and further work is being done to assess the central, best- and worst-case scenarios during the development process

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation remains a significant financial risk despite recent reductions
findings.detail: Despite the council's success in reducing temporary accommodation numbers to levels previously seen in 2013, these pressures remain a significant risk. The Renters Rights Act and Supported Housing Regulatory Oversight Act will need close tracking and are likely to lead to significant changes in commissioning, with uncertain financial impact.
findings.matters: Homelessness is demand-led and difficult to control; legislative changes (Renters Rights Act, Awaabs Law extension) may force additional costs while the financial impact remains unquantified.
findings.figures: Current expenditure level indicates 'significant risk' to financial position
findings.quote: Continued homelessness and temporary accommodation pressures remain a significant risk to the Council's financial position despite the Council's success in reducing the numbers in TA down to levels previously seen in 2013. The long term impact of the Renters Rights Act alongside the Supported Housing Regulatory Oversight Act will need to be tracked and together with the outcome of the single homeless pathway project is likely to lead to significant changes in our commissioning of providers.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Children's Services placement costs flagged as significant financial risk with ongoing volatility
findings.detail: Despite a £6.0m structural reset in 2026/27, placement volumes, mix and unit costs may exceed current MTFP assumptions. The council acknowledges a constrained and dysfunctional placement market. While the Fostering Hub and residential placement unit are expected to help, the scale and timing of financial benefits remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Placement costs are volatile and uncontrollable mid-year; this is a known weak point in the council's financial planning that could force unplanned spending increases.
findings.figures: £6.0m structural reset in 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: Children's Social Care placement costs remain a significant financial risk, with ongoing volatility in looked after children placements, care leavers and children with complex needs, alongside pressures within a constrained and dysfunctional placement market. The 2026/27 budget included a £6.0m structural reset; however, placement volumes, mix and unit costs may exceed current MTFP assumptions and require further validation.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Demand stabilisation assumption remains a challenge with continued volatility in key services
findings.detail: The council assumes demand stabilises at £10.8m per annum from 2027/28 onwards, but the paper explicitly identifies that this assumption remains challenged with continued volatility in Adult Social Care, Children's Services, homelessness/temporary accommodation and SEND. These are precisely the services driving the largest uncontrollable cost pressures.
findings.matters: If demand does not stabilise as assumed, the identified budget gaps will materially worsen, and there is limited flexibility to cut these statutory services further.
findings.figures: Demand growth assumption £10.8m per annum; 2025/26 outturn and early 2026/27 monitoring show continued volatility
findings.quote: Demand: The assumption that demand stabilises over the medium term remains a challenge, with continued volatility in certain demand led services.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix A - Exec Report MTFP 2027-32 Update Report
findings.headline: Budget gap grows from £1.1m in 2028/29 to £29.8m by 2031/32
findings.detail: The Central scenario identifies an emerging budget gap that remains limited in early years but grows significantly over time. The gap increases from £1.1m in 2028/29 to £9.8m in 2029/30, £21.4m in 2030/31, and £29.8m in 2031/32. This reflects cumulative impact of pay, inflation and demand pressures.
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit of nearly £30m by the end of the planning period signals mounting financial pressure that will require either substantial savings delivery or demand management to resolve.
findings.quote: Under the Central scenario, an emerging budget gap has been identified across the MTFP period, as illustrated in the table below. Whilst this remains relatively limited in the early years of the plan, there is a bigger gap over time, reflecting the cumulative impact of pay, inflation and demand pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £2.383m, driven by High Needs and Early Years, with ongoing SEND growth
findings.detail: The DSG (which sits outside the General Fund) shows £2.383m in-year overspend managed through DSG reserves. However, 'ongoing demand growth in SEND represents a continuing medium‑term financial challenge.' This is a non-General Fund problem that will eventually become a General Fund problem if not resolved.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a growing issue across England. Once the reserve is exhausted, councils must fund SEND from General Fund. Luton's £2.383m is a forward indicator of future General Fund pressure.
findings.figures: DSG in-year overspend: £2.383m
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) continues to present a financial risk, with an in‑year overspend of £2.383m driven primarily by High Needs and Early Years pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Commercial trading arm reported combined deficit of £0.611m, driven by Property Design Services income shortfall
findings.detail: Luton Trading Services and Schools Trading Services combined showed a £0.611m deficit, 'primarily driven by income shortfalls in Property Design Services.' Wider pressures include 'property voids, tenancy challenges and underperformance in traded services.' The council is managing this through disposal of underperforming assets, but this is treating symptoms, not root cause.
findings.matters: Commercial income volatility is a sign of market exposure. A lender should understand whether this is a one-off or a structural weakness in the council's traded offer.
findings.figures: Combined deficit: £0.611m
findings.quote: Luton Trading Services (LTS) and Schools Trading Services (STS) report a combined deficit of £0.611m, primarily driven by income shortfalls in Property Design Services.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspent by £2.36m in responsive repairs, plus £0.367m bad debt provision increase
findings.detail: The HRA faced 'increased demand, regulatory requirements and inflation' driving the repairs overspend. In addition, increased bad debt provision (£0.367m) reflects 'ongoing affordability challenges and changes in rent collection arrangements.' Together these signal both cost control and income collection challenges in the housing stock.
findings.matters: HRA overruns often herald deteriorating asset condition or tenant affordability. Both have long-term financial consequences for the council.
findings.figures: Responsive repairs overspend: £2.36m; bad debt provision increase: £0.367m
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) continues to face financial pressures, particularly within responsive repairs where increased demand, regulatory requirements and inflation have driven a £2.36m overspend at outturn.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Finance function is under-resourced with ongoing reliance on interim staff and recruitment difficulties
findings.detail: A restructure of Finance is underway to address gaps identified through external review, but 'recruitment challenges persist, and reliance on interim resources continues.' The report itself notes this 'may impact the pace of financial improvement and the sustainability of strengthened financial management arrangements.' This is particularly concerning given the forecasting accuracy problems flagged elsewhere.
findings.matters: A lender cannot place confidence in financial data, forecasting, or control if the team producing it is short-staffed and reliant on temporary cover. This is often where control fails quietly.
findings.figures: Restructure underway; recruitment challenges noted; reliance on interim resources
findings.quote: A restructure is underway to address gaps identified through external review; however, recruitment challenges persist, and reliance on interim resources continues.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Bad debt provision increased to £1.3m, reflecting 'heightened uncertainty in collection'
findings.detail: The council has formally increased its bad debt provision following a corporate review. This indicates either deteriorating collection performance or changed assumptions about what it can recover. A Debt Recovery Improvement Project is underway, but the fact that a formal review triggered a provision increase signals prior underestimation of risk.
findings.matters: Bad debt increases are a lagging indicator of household stress or collection dysfunction. Both matter to a lender; both signal deteriorating council income stability.
findings.figures: Bad debt provision: £1.3m (increased following corporate review)
findings.quote: At outturn, the bad debt provision has increased to £1.3m following a corporate review reflecting heightened uncertainty in collection.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £1.52m in purchased care and demographic growth, with ongoing volatility
findings.detail: The second-largest service overspend reflects pressures in purchased care services, demographic growth, and increased bad debt provision. Although improved compared to earlier in the year, the report states 'both service areas remain subject to ongoing demand pressures, cost volatility and continued financial recovery planning.'
findings.matters: ASC demand is nationally volatile and growing. A council showing £1.52m here is exposed to further cost growth unless it can demonstrate control of placement strategies and unit costs.
findings.figures: £1.52m overspend in Adult Social Care
findings.quote: Adult Social Care reports an overspend of £1.52m, primarily reflecting pressures in purchased care services, demographic growth, and increased bad debt provision.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Capital programme shows £216.1m slippage (70% of all schemes), signalling governance and delivery risk
findings.detail: Massive delays across housing, regeneration, and transport programmes, including Denbigh Primary School where costs are forecast to exceed the approved budget. The report notes this raises 'risks relating to cost escalation, delivery capacity, and the timing and certainty of funding' and calls for strengthened business case development and Prudential Code compliance. This is not a one-off slip; it is systemic.
findings.matters: Large slippage often signals cost creep (scope expansion), weak project management, or affordability failure. A lender depends on knowing whether capital forecasts can be trusted.
findings.figures: £216.1m programme slippage; approximately 70% of the capital programme
findings.quote: Programme slippage totals £216.1m (approximately 70% of the capital programme), reflecting delays in delivery across major schemes.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Savings delivery target missed by 21%: £1.5m undelivered and £0.8m deferred to next year
findings.detail: Of £10.7m in planned savings for 2025/26, only £8.4m materialised. £1.5m of savings never delivered at all, and a further £0.8m pushed into 2026/27. The report identifies delays in transformation delivery and 'challenges in achieving third-party spend reductions' as the root cause. This compounds the reliance on reserves since savings plans are not meeting their targets.
findings.matters: If a council cannot hit its planned savings, future budget projections lose credibility. This is often the first sign of a widening structural deficit.
findings.figures: £10.7m target; £8.4m delivered (78%); £1.5m undelivered; £0.8m deferred into 2026/27
findings.quote: Of the £10.7m savings target for 2025/26, £8.4m has been delivered at outturn, with £0.8m deferred into 2026/27 and £1.5m remaining undelivered.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Children's Services overspent by £5.842m, driven by persistent placement cost pressures and asylum-seeking children demand
findings.detail: This is the largest service pressure and reflects sustained high costs across residential care, semi-independent accommodation, support for children with disabilities, and unaccompanied asylum-seeking children. The report notes this as 'the most significant financial risk to the Council's budget position' and does not indicate the underlying drivers are being brought under control.
findings.matters: This is a high-volatility, growing cost area that shows no sign of stabilisation. A lender needs to understand whether this reflects demographic inevitability or service failure.
findings.figures: £5.842m overspend; described as 'sustained high placement costs'
findings.quote: Children's Services report an overspend of £5.842m, driven by sustained high placement costs across residential care, semi‑independent accommodation, and support for children with disabilities, alongside pressures relating to unaccompanied asylum‑seeking children.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Outturn Budget Risks & Financial Management
findings.headline: Balanced outturn is entirely dependent on depleting contingency reserves, not sustainable action
findings.detail: The council reported a balanced £176.1m budget for 2025/26, but this required drawing down £6.6m of contingency and £0.154m from reserves to cover in-year pressures. The report explicitly states: 'the underlying financial position therefore remains structurally challenged' and notes the position 'has been supported through the use of contingency and reserve funding, alongside in‑year mitigation actions.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a balanced budget reflects genuine operational improvement or merely defers problems. This council has used its shock absorber rather than fixed its pressures.
findings.figures: £6.643m contingency fully utilised; £6.6m drawn down in-year; £0.154m from reserves; net improvement of £6.7m vs Q3 forecast achieved only via these drawdowns
findings.quote: The Council holds £6.643m in General Fund contingencies, which have been fully utilised during 2025/26 to address demand‑led pressures and exceptional cost pressures, contributing to the achievement of a balanced outturn.

findings.paper_title: 8a. Appendix A - Luton Borough Council - Audit Progress Report and Sector Updates
findings.headline: Auditor does not expect to issue an unmodified audit opinion for 2025/26 financial statements
findings.detail: Grant Thornton explicitly states they do not expect to be able to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements in advance of the backstop date. They indicate priority is gaining assurance over in-year transactions and closing balances only.
findings.matters: A qualified or disclaimed audit opinion for a third consecutive year would indicate the council remains unable to produce auditable financial statements and continue undermining lender confidence.
findings.figures: Expected outcome for 2025/26 (deadline 31 January 2027, audit to be completed by 30 November 2026)
findings.quote: we do not expect to be able to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements in advance of the backstop date

findings.paper_title: 8a. Appendix A - Luton Borough Council - Audit Progress Report and Sector Updates
findings.headline: Unresolved transaction mapping issue remains outstanding ahead of September audit visit
findings.detail: During initial audit work starting 15 June 2026, Grant Thornton identified a challenge in resolving the mapping of transaction listings to the accounts, which is needed to progress audit work on journals. This mapping issue remains unresolved, though the council agreed to resolve it before the next audit visit in September.
findings.matters: Unresolved transaction mapping indicates weaknesses in the general ledger reconciliation process and the ability to trace transactions through the financial system, creating uncertainty about the accuracy of reported figures.
findings.figures: Identified during initial four-week audit period starting 15 June 2026; to be resolved by September 2026
findings.quote: A challenge during this period was resolving the mapping of a small number of transaction listings to the accounts, which is needed to progress our work on journals. This mapping issue remains unresolved but the Council has agreed to resolve this before our next visit in September.

findings.paper_title: 8a. Appendix A - Luton Borough Council - Audit Progress Report and Sector Updates
findings.headline: Poor quality of draft accounts and working papers persists despite improvements noted in 2024/25
findings.detail: Significant issues were identified during the 2023/24 audit revealing poor quality of draft accounts and working papers. While improvements were noted in 2024/25, the same factors were still being identified, indicating ongoing problems with financial statement preparation.
findings.matters: Poor quality working papers and draft accounts indicate weak financial reporting processes and controls, increasing audit risk and the likelihood of material errors in financial statements.
findings.figures: Issues identified in 2023/24, recurrence in 2024/25
